summary: Gives the profile for DCCP Congestion Control ID 3, which uses TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC). It suits senders that want a sending rate comparable to TCP's, possibly with Explicit Congestion Notification, while avoiding abrupt rate changes. It is standards-track and was later updated by several RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4342 defines one way for DCCP connections to adjust how quickly they send data. It aims to share network capacity fairly while changing the sending rate less abruptly than TCP-like control.

questions: how does tfrc calculate sending rate
how does tfrc set the sending rate
subtitle: A DCCP profile that adjusts sending speed smoothly using receiver reports of packet loss.

tldr.problem: Some applications need a sending rate that shares bandwidth fairly with TCP but changes less abruptly. TCP-like control cuts its rate sharply after congestion.
tldr.mechanism: CCID 3 uses TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC). The sender estimates a fair rate from reported loss intervals, round-trip time, and packet size.
tldr.outcome: The smoother rate comes with slower response to bandwidth changes. RFC 4342 has been updated by RFC 5348, RFC 6323, and RFC 8311.

today: RFC 4342 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5348, RFC 6323, and RFC 8311.

sections.title: What CCID 3 Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4342 defines Congestion Control Identifier 3 (CCID 3) for the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP). A CCID selects the congestion-control method for one direction of a DCCP connection. CCID 3 uses TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC), a receiver-based method that adjusts the sender's permitted rate using the rate of loss events.

The RFC says CCID 3 is suitable when an application prefers a smooth rate, including streaming media with small or moderate receiver buffering. Compared with TCP-like congestion control, it changes rate less abruptly but responds more slowly when available bandwidth changes. Applications that mainly need to transfer as much data as possible quickly are directed to TCP-like control instead.
sections.plainLanguage: CCID 3 is for data flows that benefit from a steady sending speed. It shares network capacity fairly, but it reacts more slowly when conditions change.

sections.title: How the Sender Sets Its Rate
sections.content:
The sender uses a loss-event rate, a round-trip-time estimate, and an average packet size in the TCP throughput equation defined by RFC 3448. The result is the fair sending rate that limits the sender. At the start, the sender uses slow start and roughly doubles its permitted rate each round-trip time until the receiver reports a dropped or marked data packet.

CCID 3 allows an initial rate of at least two and at most four packets per round-trip time, with the larger initial rates limited by the byte limit specified in RFC 3390. The sender also limits its rate to at most twice the receiver's reported receive rate. A no-feedback timer reduces the permitted rate by half if required feedback does not arrive; the rate does not fall below one packet per 64 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender uses packet-loss reports and timing information to calculate a fair sending speed. If reports stop arriving, it reduces that speed.

sections.title: Receiver Feedback and Loss Intervals
sections.content:
The receiver normally sends feedback about once per round-trip time when data arrives that often. Required feedback includes an acknowledgement number, elapsed-time information, the Receive Rate option, and the Loss Intervals option. The sender uses the reported intervals to calculate a loss-event rate and update its permitted rate.

A loss interval starts with a lost or ECN-marked data packet. Its lossy part covers no more than one round-trip time, and its lossless part contains later data packets that were not dropped or marked. The receiver uses the packet window counter to decide whether losses belong to one event and when to send more feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver reports how much data arrived and where losses occurred. The sender uses those reports to adjust its sending speed.

sections.title: Options and Explicit Congestion Notification
sections.content:
CCID 3 defines three options: Loss Event Rate (type 192), Loss Intervals (type 193), and Receive Rate (type 194). The Loss Intervals option can report up to 28 recent intervals, although TFRC currently uses at most the latest 9. These CCID 3 options must be ignored when they appear on DCCP-Data packets.

CCID 3 supports Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN). When ECN is used, the receiver returns ECN Nonce information in the Loss Intervals option. The sender can use that information to check probabilistically whether the receiver reported losses and marks correctly. The sender can also compare reported intervals with its own window-counter records.
sections.plainLanguage: Three DCCP options carry the receiver's loss and delivery-rate reports. ECN nonce information gives the sender a way to check some of those reports.

sections.title: Security and Status Today
sections.content:
The RFC refers to DCCP and TFRC for general security considerations, including spoofed feedback and incorrect receiver reports. It describes the ECN Nonce as a way for the sender to check feedback; without ECN, occasional packet choices can also expose some false reporting, but less robustly and less unobtrusively.

RFC 4342 is a Proposed Standard. Unit metadata lists later updates in RFC 5348, RFC 6323, and RFC 8311, so those updates should be read with this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can check some receiver reports, but feedback can still be spoofed or inaccurate. RFC 4342 has later updates that readers should consider alongside it.
